---
title: Checking Untrusted Code
---

Sometimes you have to look at a repository you did not write, such as a
package submitted for review. You want to know what state it is in without
running anything it contains. The `triage` profile is made for that.

## The Command

```bash
timeout 120 pycmdcheck --profile triage --json --exit-zero path/to/repo > report.json
```

Each part has a reason.

| Part | Reason |
|------|--------|
| `timeout 120` | Stops the run after 120 seconds. `timeout` is part of GNU coreutils. See [Limits](#limits). |
| `--profile triage` | Runs only the checks that read files |
| `--json` | Prints a report another program can read |
| `--exit-zero` | Makes the exit code say whether pycmdcheck ran, not what it found |
| `path/to/repo` | Names the repository as an argument, so pycmdcheck is not started from inside it |

To use pycmdcheck without installing it, run it through `uvx`.

```bash
uvx pycmdcheck --profile triage path/to/repo
```

## What the Profile Runs and Leaves Out

The profile runs 12 checks, which are `changelog`, `ci`, `citation`,
`community`, `docs`, `license`, `metadata`, `py_typed`, `python_versions`,
`structure`, `test_suite` and `version`. Each of them reads files and nothing
else. They install nothing, start no other program and open no network
connection.

Two of them answer questions that a reviewer would otherwise need to run
something for.

- `test_suite` says whether the repository has tests. It looks for test
  directories and test files and does not run them. A repository with none
  gets a warning with the code `test_suite.missing`.
- `docs` says whether there is documentation beyond the README. It looks for
  the setup of a site builder such as Sphinx or MkDocs, for pages in a `docs/`
  directory, and for a documentation link in the metadata. A repository with
  none gets a note with the code `docs.missing-site`.

[Configuration](configuration.qmd#test_suite) lists what each of the two
looks for.

The other eight built-in checks are left out.

| Check | Why it is left out |
|-------|--------------------|
| `tests`, `doctests` | They run the project's tests and doctests, which executes its code. Whether there are tests at all is reported by `test_suite`. |
| `build` | It runs the project's build, which executes its code |
| `linting`, `typing` | They start tools that read the project's configuration, and that configuration can name a plugin or a start-up hook for the tool to load |
| `formatting` | It starts a formatter, which has to be installed |
| `dependencies` | It reads the metadata of the packages installed next to pycmdcheck to learn which modules a dependency provides, so the answer depends on your environment |
| `urls` | It sends requests to addresses the repository chose. It refuses [local and private hosts](configuration.qmd#local-and-private-hosts), connects only to the address it tested, and follows a redirect only to another `http` or `https` address. It still contacts any public host the repository names, and behind a proxy the proxy looks the names up. |

The repository cannot change this selection, and no setting in the
`[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of its `pyproject.toml` changes a result.

- An enable flag in that table, such as `license = false`, does not take a
  check out of the profile.
- `docs` is the only one of the 12 checks that has options, and the profile
  sets all five of them. They are `require_readme`, `check_readme_sections`,
  `check_docs_site`, `check_docstrings` and `min_docstring_coverage`. The
  repository's values for them are ignored. It can neither relax what is
  asked of the README nor switch the docstring scan on.
- Custom checks are outside every profile, so none runs here even when one is
  installed. The deprecated `imports` check is in no profile either.

One setting in that table still acts. When you do not pass `--fail-on`, the
repository's [`fail_on`](configuration.qmd#fail_on) list is used, and it then
decides three things.

- The exit code of your run.
- The `fail_on` and `failed` keys of the JSON report.
- The closing line of the text and Markdown reports.

It can only make the run stricter, because an error fails the run under
every setting. `--exit-zero` takes the exit code away and leaves the other
two. Pass `--fail-on` yourself to take all three away, or read `passed` and
`summary`, which no setting changes.

A settings file given with [`--config`](cli.qmd#config-file) takes even that
away. The `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of the repository is then not read at
all. Its `fail_on` has no effect, and no warning about the table is printed.
[A workflow with a settings file](#workflow-settings-file) below shows one
in use.

## How to Start pycmdcheck

Use the `pycmdcheck` command and pass the repository as `PATH`, as shown
above. `python -P -m pycmdcheck` is equally safe. The `-P` option keeps the
current directory off Python's module search path.

Do not change into the repository and run `python -m pycmdcheck` there. Python
then puts the current directory first on its module search path. pycmdcheck
removes that entry when it starts, which stops a repository from supplying
its own checks. The removal comes too late for the modules Python has loaded
by then, so a file in the repository named like one of those modules would be
loaded in its place.

## Limits {#limits}

pycmdcheck reads regular files only, and each read stops at a size cap. A text
file such as the README or the license is read up to 1 mebibyte (MiB), which
is 1,048,576 bytes. A `pyproject.toml` larger than 1 MiB is treated as
unreadable. A Python file larger than 2 MiB is skipped and named in the
report. So is a Python file the parser cannot read, for example one whose
expressions are nested too deeply.

Two things are not bounded, and that is why the run needs limits from outside.

- **Time.** A file built to be slow for the Python parser is not detected.
  Give the run a time limit, as `timeout` does above. When the limit is
  reached, `timeout` exits with code 124 and `report.json` is empty.
- **Memory.** Parsing needs far more memory than the file is large. By the
  measurement recorded in pycmdcheck's source, a Python file at the 2 MiB cap
  can need about 1.3 GB while it is parsed, and up to four checks run at the
  same time. Give the run a memory limit, and add `--no-parallel` to keep the
  peak lower.

How you set a memory limit depends on the system. A container or a virtual
machine with a memory cap works everywhere. On Linux, `ulimit -v` with a size
in kibibytes, given in the same shell before the command, caps what the run
may reserve. macOS rejects that command.

Treat a missing or empty report as "not checked". It is never a clean result.

## Reading the Report

The report is one JSON object. The
[command-line reference](cli.qmd#json-output) describes every key. This is the
report for a small package whose `pyproject.toml` has a table header that is
never closed. The path is shortened, and 10 of the 12 results are left out.

```json
{
  "package_path": ".../broken",
  "passed": false,
  "summary": {
    "ok": 5,
    "note": 4,
    "warning": 0,
    "error": 1,
    "skipped": 2
  },
  "results": [
    {
      "name": "metadata",
      "status": "error",
      "message": "Invalid pyproject.toml",
      "details": [
        "TOML parse error: Expected ']' at the end of a table declaration (at line 18, column 14)"
      ],
      "duration": 5.364418029785156e-05,
      "findings": [
        {
          "code": "metadata.unreadable-pyproject",
          "status": "error",
          "message": "TOML parse error: Expected ']' at the end of a table declaration (at line 18, column 14)",
          "hint": "Correct pyproject.toml so that it is valid TOML, saved as UTF-8 with no byte order mark."
        }
      ],
      "skip_reason": null
    },
    {
      "name": "python_versions",
      "status": "skipped",
      "message": "pyproject.toml could not be read",
      "details": [
        "The metadata check reports the reason"
      ],
      "duration": 0.0002830028533935547,
      "findings": [],
      "skip_reason": "prerequisite-failed"
    }
  ],
  "schema_version": 1,
  "pycmdcheck_version": "0.2.0",
  "profile": "triage",
  "config_file": null,
  "fail_on": [
    "error"
  ],
  "failed": true,
  "requested_checks": null,
  "skipped_checks": []
}
```

The eight keys after `results` describe the run. `schema_version` is `1` for
this layout, so a program can test it before it reads anything else.
`profile` names the profile that was given, and `requested_checks` is `null`
when the run used that profile's own set of checks. A program that needs to
know the run stayed inside `triage` tests both, because `--check` on the
command line, or `-c` for short, can name a check outside the profile.
`config_file` is `null` because the run was given no `--config` file. With
one it holds the path of the file as it was written on the command line.
`failed` says whether the run would have exited with code 1 without
`--exit-zero`. It is `true` here because of the one error.

### What a Program Should Read

Each result is read in three steps.

1. Read `status`. It is one of the five values in the table below.
2. For a `skipped` result, read `skip_reason`. It says why the check did not
   look at anything, and it is one of nine fixed values.
3. For a `note`, a `warning` or an `error`, read the `code` of each entry of
   `findings`. A code names the rule the finding comes from, and a result can
   carry several findings.

The codes and the skip reasons are stable names, and
[Rule Codes](rules.qmd) lists them all. The `message` and the `details` are
written for people, and so is the `hint` of a finding, which is one sentence
on what to do about it. Show them to the reviewer, and do not compare their
text, because the wording can change. `findings` and `skip_reason` are new in
version 0.2.0.

These lines of Python print the skipped checks with their reasons and group
the findings by code.

```python
import json

with open("report.json", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    report = json.load(handle)

print(report["summary"])
by_code = {}
for result in report["results"]:
    if result["status"] == "skipped":
        print("skipped:", result["name"], "because", result["skip_reason"])
    for finding in result["findings"]:
        by_code.setdefault(finding["code"], []).append(finding)

for code, findings in sorted(by_code.items()):
    print(f"{findings[0]['status']}: {code} ({len(findings)})")
```

```
{'ok': 5, 'note': 4, 'warning': 0, 'error': 1, 'skipped': 2}
skipped: python_versions because prerequisite-failed
skipped: version because prerequisite-failed
note: ci.missing (1)
note: citation.missing (1)
note: community.missing-code-of-conduct (1)
note: community.missing-contributing (1)
error: metadata.unreadable-pyproject (1)
note: py_typed.missing (1)
```

The reason `prerequisite-failed` says that another check reports the cause.
Here that check is `metadata`, with the code `metadata.unreadable-pyproject`.
A program can therefore count the broken `pyproject.toml` once and not three
times.

### The Five Statuses

| Status | What it means for a reviewer |
|--------|------------------------------|
| `ok` | The check found what it looked for |
| `note` | Something the author can improve, such as adding a citation file. Worth a mention, and not a defect in itself. |
| `warning` | A likely problem, such as a missing license file, a missing README or a repository with no tests. Look at it. |
| `error` | The check failed. Under this profile that means the metadata is missing, cannot be read, or lacks a name or version, no importable package was found, or the version in the code differs from the one in the metadata. |
| `skipped` | The check did not look at anything, and `skip_reason` says why. This is not a pass. |

A check that has nothing to look at is always skipped. It never returns a
note or ok for that. Under this profile the reason is `not-applicable` when
the project has nothing of the kind, as a single module has no package
directory for `py_typed`. It is `prerequisite-failed` when another check
reports what is missing. A third reason, `parse-failed`, says that `py_typed`
or `version` could not parse the code, for example because the repository
uses syntax newer than the Python that runs pycmdcheck.

An error whose finding has a code that starts with `pycmdcheck` and a dot is a
fault in pycmdcheck and not a finding about the repository. The `name` of
that result is still the name of the check that failed.

[Configuration](configuration.qmd#statuses-each-check-can-return) lists the
statuses each check can return.

### Exit Codes

With `--exit-zero` the exit code describes the run and not the repository.

| Code | Meaning | Standard output |
|------|---------|-----------------|
| 0 | pycmdcheck ran | The JSON report |
| 2 | Usage error, for example a path that does not exist or a mistake in a `--config` file | Empty |
| 3 | pycmdcheck itself failed | Empty |

Without `--exit-zero`, any error in the report would give exit code 1. When
you pass neither `--fail-on` nor `--config`, so would any other status the
repository names in its own `fail_on` setting. A caller would then have to
tell code 1 apart from codes 2 and 3 to know whether there is a report. With
the option, a non-zero code always means there is no report to read.

## A pyproject.toml That Does Not Parse

A broken `pyproject.toml` does not stop the run. The report above shows what
happens.

- `metadata` returns the one `error`, with the code
  `metadata.unreadable-pyproject` and the parser's message in `details`.
- `python_versions` and `version`, which need the file, are `skipped` with the
  reason `prerequisite-failed` and point at `metadata`.
- The other nine checks run as usual.
- A warning goes to standard error, standard output is still valid JSON, and
  with `--exit-zero` the exit code is 0.

A file that is not valid UTF-8, and a `pyproject.toml` that is a directory,
give the same three results. A repository with no `pyproject.toml`,
`setup.py` or `setup.cfg` gives the same pattern, with the code
`metadata.missing` on the error.

A `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table with a malformed `fail_on` or a malformed check
entry also gives an ordinary report, with one warning on standard error for
each kind of mistake. An option of the wrong type inside a check's table
gives no warning. [Configuration](configuration.qmd#basic-configuration) says
what happens to it.

Each of these warnings is one line. A line about the words in a `fail_on`
list, or about the entries under `checks`, names the ones that have the
mistake. It names at most 25 of them and then gives a count, so a table full
of mistakes adds a few lines to the log of your job and not hundreds. A
`fail_on` that is not a list gives a line that names the key and the type it
found, and so does a `checks` value that is not a table. Text that a warning
quotes from the table is cleaned first. A line break or another control
character in it is shown as an escape such as `\n`, so the repository cannot
write lines of its own to standard error. A value that is too large to
print, such as a number with thousands of digits, is named as
`a value too large to show` and does not end the run.

With `--config` none of these warnings is printed, the one for a
`pyproject.toml` that does not parse included, because the table is not
read. The `metadata` check still reports the broken file in its result.

## Posting a Comment {#posting-a-comment}

A program that answers on a pull request or an issue can ask for the report
as Markdown and post the file as it is.

```bash
timeout 120 pycmdcheck --profile triage --fail-on error --format markdown --exit-zero --output report.md path/to/repo
```

`--fail-on error` keeps the closing line of the report yours. Without it the
repository's own `fail_on` setting decides whether that line says the run
failed. `--output` writes the report to `report.md` and prints nothing on
standard output. The report has a table with one row for each check, and a
collapsed block for each result that is not ok and has detail lines or
hints. The block lists each hint after the detail lines, as an item that
starts with `**Suggestion:**`, so the comment gives the author of the
package a suggestion for each finding. A suggestion here and the `hint` of a
finding in the JSON report are the same sentence. The
[command-line reference](cli.qmd#markdown-output) shows such a report.

The file is written once, when the run is over. When the run fails or is
stopped, nothing is written, and a `report.md` from an earlier run stays as it
was. Remove the old file before the run, and post the new one only when the
exit code is 0.

Text from the repository is meant to be shown as text and not read as
Markdown. A message, a detail line or a hint may quote a file name, a version
or a metadata value that the repository chose. The report puts each such text
on one line and puts a backslash before the characters that Markdown reads as
markup, so the text cannot break the table, write a Markdown link or start a
heading. It also places a zero-width space, which is an invisible character,
after every `@` and inside anything shaped like `:word:`. The comment then
notifies no user or team and shows no emoji.

A repository whose `requires-python` is `@octocat :tada: | >=3.11` gets this
block for its `metadata` result. The first item is a detail line that quotes
the value, and the second is the suggestion. Here `<U+200B>` stands for the
zero-width space, which the file holds as a character you cannot see.

```
<details>
<summary>metadata: note</summary>

- requires-python is not a valid version specifier: '@<U+200B>octocat :<U+200B>tada: \| \>=3.11'
- **Suggestion:** Set requires-python in the \[project\] table of pyproject.toml to a value such as "\>=3.12".

</details>
```

A web address gets the same invisible character after `https:` or `www`, so
GitHub shows it as text and the comment holds no link that the repository
chose. GitHub may still link a few kinds of plain text, such as an issue
reference written as `GH-1`.

The Markdown report is for people to read. A program that has to decide
something should run the JSON command as well and read that report.

### In a GitHub Actions Workflow {#github-actions}

Two steps are enough for a bot that comments on an issue. They come after
the steps that fetch the submitted repository into `submitted-package` and
install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

```yaml
- name: Run pycmdcheck
  run: |
    timeout 120 uvx pycmdcheck@0.2.0 --profile triage --fail-on error \
      --format markdown --exit-zero --output report.md submitted-package

- name: Post the report
  env:
    GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
    ISSUE: ${{ github.event.issue.number }}
  run: |
    gh issue comment "$ISSUE" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \
      --body-file report.md --edit-last --create-if-none
```

The profile chooses the checks and the Markdown report is the comment, so the
workflow holds no list of checks and no code that reads the results. A later
release can add a check to the profile and the bot picks it up when the
version in the first step is raised. Name a version there, so that the
comments change only when you decide to update.

The second step runs only when the first one succeeds, which is when the
report was written. `--edit-last` replaces the bot's earlier comment on the
issue and `--create-if-none` writes a first one, so the issue holds one
report however often the workflow runs. The job needs the permission
`issues: write`, and a recent GitHub command line tool for
`--create-if-none`.

A bot that does not want every check of the profile adds `--skip` to the
first step. Several names go in one value, separated by commas.

```yaml
- name: Run pycmdcheck
  run: |
    timeout 120 uvx pycmdcheck@0.2.0 --profile triage --fail-on error \
      --skip citation,community \
      --format markdown --exit-zero --output report.md submitted-package
```

Write no space after a comma. The shell ends the value at a space, so
pycmdcheck would stop with exit code 2 and write no report, and nothing
would be posted. `--skip` can also be given once for each name.

#### With a Settings File {#workflow-settings-file}

The step that runs pycmdcheck holds the bot's whole selection in one
command, and for most bots that is enough. A settings file is worth having
when that command grows, or when the bot has to set an option of a check,
which cannot be done on the command line. The file is kept in the bot's own
repository, so a change to what the bot checks is a change to one small file
that can be reviewed. It is written in TOML (Tom's Obvious Minimal
Language), the format of `pyproject.toml`.

```toml
# .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml, in the bot's own repository
profile = "triage"
fail_on = "warning"

[checks]
citation = false
```

Only the first step changes. `--config` takes the place of `--profile` and
`--fail-on`, because the file now holds both. The second step stays as it
is.

```yaml
- name: Run pycmdcheck
  run: |
    timeout 120 uvx pycmdcheck@0.2.0 --config .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml \
      --format markdown --exit-zero --output report.md submitted-package
```

The job has to check out the bot's own repository before this step, so that
the file is in the working directory. When the file is not there, pycmdcheck
exits with code 2 and writes no report. This is the last line it writes to
standard error.

```
Error: Invalid value for '--config': File '.github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml' does not exist.
```

With this file the comment changes in three places. The report has no
`citation` row, and its closing line says that the run failed when a check
returns a warning or an error. The line under the heading names the file
beside the profile. The `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of the submitted
repository is not read, so no setting of that repository reaches the
comment.

A mistake in the file ends the first step with exit code 2. No report is
written, the second step does not run, and nothing is posted. To test a
changed file before it is merged, run
`pycmdcheck --config .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml --list` in the bot's
repository. That reads the file, runs no check and needs no submitted
package. [Configuration](configuration.qmd#config-file) is the reference for
the file.
